# AF 第八章 原文（重制基线）

## Chapter 8

[P01] A few days later, the fear from the killings（杀戮） went away. In Chapter 8, some animals remembered, or thought they did, that the Sixth Commandment（戒律） said, "No animal shall kill any other animal."No one wanted to say this near the pigs or dogs, but they felt the killings were wrong. Clover asked Benjamin to read her the Sixth Commandment（戒律）. He said he would not interfere（干涉）, so she brought Muriel. Muriel read it: "No animal shall kill any other animal WITHOUT CAUSE." The last two words had somehow left the animals' memory.

[P02] But now they saw that the Commandment had not been broken. There was clearly a good reason to kill the traitors who had joined Snowball. All through the year the animals worked even harder than before. They had to rebuild the windmill（风车） with thicker walls and finish it by the set date, along with the usual farm work. It was a tremendous（极大的） labour. Sometimes it seemed to them that they worked longer hours and ate no better than in Jones's day. On Sunday mornings Squealer held down a long strip（剥去） of paper and read out lists of numbers. These proved that the production of every kind of food had gone up by two hundred, three hundred, or five hundred per cent.

[P03] The animals did not doubt him. They could not remember clearly what life was like before the uprising（起义）. Still, some days they wished for less numbers and more food. Now all orders came from Squealer or another pig. Napoleon was not seen in public even once in two weeks. When he did appear, dogs went with him, and a black cockerel（小公鸡） marched in front. It acted like a trumpeter, giving a loud "cock（公鸡）-a-doodle（涂鸦）-doo（嘟嘟）" before Napoleon spoke.

[P04] Even in the farmhouse（农舍）, they said, Napoleon lived in rooms apart（分开） from the others. He ate alone, with two dogs to serve him, and always used the Crown（王冠） Derby（德比） dinner set from the glass cupboard（橱柜） in the drawing-room. They also announced that the gun would fire every year on Napoleon's birthday, and on the other two anniversaries（周年）. People never spoke of him simply as "Napoleon." They always called him in formal style "our Leader, Comrade（同志） Napoleon," and the pigs liked to make up titles for him like Father of All Animals, Terror（恐怖） of Mankind, Protector（保护者） of the Sheep-fold, Ducklings（小鸭）' Friend, and so on.

[P05] In his speeches, Squealer would talk with tears about Napoleon's wisdom, the goodness of his heart, and his deep love for all animals, especially the unhappy animals who still lived with no knowledge and slavery（奴役） on other farms. People now gave Napoleon the credit（功劳） for every success and every piece of good luck. You would often hear one hen say to another, "Under the guidance of our Leader, Comrade（同志） Napoleon, I have laid five eggs in six days"; or two cows, drinking at the pool, would exclaim（惊叫）, "Thanks to the leadership（领导） of Comrade Napoleon, how excellent this water tastes!" The general feeling was well expressed in a poem called Comrade Napoleon, which Minimus wrote, and which went like this: Friend of fatherless（无父）!

[P06] Fountain（喷泉） of happiness! Lord（老爷） of the swill（泔水）-bucket! Oh, how my soul is on fire when I look at your calm and commanding（指挥） eye, like the sun in the sky, Comrade Napoleon! You give all that your creatures（生物） love, a full belly（肚子） twice a day, clean straw（稻草） to roll upon; every beast（野兽）, great or small, sleeps in peace in his stall（畜栏）, you watch over all, Comrade Napoleon! If I had a sucking（吸奶）-pig, before he had grown as big as a pint（品脱） bottle or a rolling-pin（擀面杖）, he should have learned to be faithful（忠诚） and true to you. Yes, his first squeak（叫声） should be "Comrade Napoleon!" Napoleon approved（批准） of this poem and had it written on the wall of the big barn（谷仓）, at the opposite end from the Seven Commandments（戒律）.

[P07] On top was a picture of Napoleon, in profile（侧面）, painted by Squealer in white. Meanwhile（同时）, through Whymper, Napoleon was having long, hard talks with Frederick and Pilkington. The wood was still not sold. Frederick wanted it more, but would not pay a fair price. At the same time, new rumours（谣言） said Frederick planned to attack Animal Farm and destroy the windmill, because it made him jealous. Snowball was said to be hiding on Pinchfield（窄地） Farm. In the middle of summer, the animals were frightened to hear that three hens had admitted（承认） joining a plot（阴谋） to kill Napoleon.

[P08] They killed the three hens at once, and Napoleon took steps to keep safe. Four dogs guarded his bed at night, one at each corner. A young pig called Pinkeye（红眼） tasted all his food first, in case it was poisoned（中毒）. People said Napoleon would sell the pile of timber（木材） to Mr. Pilkington, and make a regular agreement to exchange products between Animal Farm and Foxwood（狐林）. Napoleon and Pilkington seemed almost friendly, though they only talked through Whymper.

[P09] The animals did not trust Pilkington, because he was a human, but they liked him much more than Frederick, whom they feared and hated. As the summer went on and the windmill was almost finished, rumours of an attack grew stronger. People said Frederick wanted to bring twenty men with guns. He had already bribed（贿赂） the judges and police, so if he got the title-deeds（事迹） of Animal Farm, they would ask no questions. Also, terrible stories came out of Pinchfield about Frederick's cruel acts. He had beaten an old horse to death, starved（饿死） his cows, killed a dog by throwing it into the furnace（火炉）, and made cocks（公鸡） fight with razor（剃刀） pieces tied to their spurs（马刺）.

[P10] When the animals heard of these things done to their comrades（同志们）, their blood boiled with anger. Sometimes they cried out to be allowed to go out together and attack Pinchfield Farm, drive out the humans, and set the animals free. But Squealer told them to avoid rash（轻率） actions and trust in Comrade Napoleon's strategy. Still, feeling against Frederick stayed strong. One Sunday morning Napoleon came into the barn and explained that he had never thought of selling the pile of timber to Frederick. He said it was beneath（在下面） his dignity（尊严） to deal with scoundrels（恶棍） of that kind.

[P11] The pigeons still flew out to spread news of the uprising. They must not land on Foxwood, and must stop saying "Death to Humanity（人类）." They must say "Death to Frederick" instead. In late summer, another of Snowball's secret plans was found. The wheat crop was full of weeds（杂草）. Snowball had come at night and mixed weed seeds with the seed corn. A gander（雄鹅） knew this, told Squealer he was guilty, then killed himself by eating deadly nightshade（颠茄） berries（浆果）. The animals also learned that Snowball had never received "Animal Hero, First Class." That was only a story he spread himself after the Battle of the Cowshed（牛棚）.

[P12] He was not given any honour. Instead, he was blamed（责备） for being a coward（懦夫） in the battle. Some animals felt puzzled（困惑） when they heard this, but Squealer soon made them believe their memories were wrong. In the autumn, the windmill was finished. It took a tremendous (极大的) and exhausting（累人） effort, because the harvest had to be gathered（聚集） at almost the same time. The machines still had to be put in, and Whymper was talking about buying them, but the building itself was complete.

[P13] They had met every difficulty. They had no experience, only simple tools, bad luck and Snowball's treachery（背叛）, but the work was finished on the very day they had planned! Tired but proud, the animals walked round their masterpiece（杰作）. To them it looked even more beautiful than the first windmill. Moreover, the walls were twice as thick as before. Only explosives（炸药） could bring them down! They thought of all their labour and the great change in their lives when the sails turned and the dynamos（发电机） ran. Then their tiredness（疲劳） left them. They jumped and ran round the windmill, shouting with triumph（胜利）.

[P14] Napoleon himself, with his dogs and his cockerel, came down to look at the finished work. He personally praised the animals for their success, and said the mill（磨坊） would be named Napoleon Mill. Two days later, the animals were called to a special meeting in the barn. They were too surprised to speak when Napoleon said he had sold the pile of timber to Frederick. Tomorrow Frederick's wagons（货车） would come and begin to take it away. All through the time when he seemed to be friends with Pilkington, Napoleon had really been in secret agreement with Frederick. All relations with Foxwood were broken off; insulting（侮辱） messages had been sent to Pilkington.

[P15] The pigeons were told to stay away from Pinchfield Farm. Their slogan changed from "Death to Frederick" to "Death to Pilkington." Napoleon also told the animals that the stories of a coming attack were not true. He said the tales about Frederick being cruel were much worse than the truth. All these rumours probably came from Snowball and his agents. It now seemed that Snowball was not hiding on Pinchfield Farm after all.** In fact, he had never been there in his life. He was living at Foxwood—in great luxury（奢侈）—and had been supported by Pilkington for years. The pigs were very happy about Napoleon's clever plan.

[P16] By seeming friendly with Pilkington, he made Frederick raise his price by twelve pounds. But Squealer said Napoleon's great mind showed in this: he trusted nobody, not even Frederick. Frederick wanted to pay for the timber with a cheque（支票）—a piece of paper promising to pay. But Napoleon was too clever. He asked for real five-pound notes, to be given before the timber was taken away. Frederick had already paid. The money was just enough to buy the machinery（机器） for the windmill. Meanwhile（同时） the timber was carried away at high speed.

[P17] When the timber was gone, the animals had a special meeting in the barn. They came to look at Frederick's bank-notes. Napoleon sat on straw on the platform（舞台）, smiling happily and wearing both his medals. The money was by his side, neatly（整洁地） piled on a china dish. The animals walked slowly past in a line, and each looked as long as he wanted. Boxer put out his nose to smell the bank-notes, and the thin white things moved and made a small noise in his breath. Three days later there was a terrible noise. Whymper came racing up the path（小路） on his bicycle, his face very white. He threw it down in the yard and rushed straight into the farmhouse.

[P18] The next moment a choking（窒息） roar（吼叫） of anger came from Napoleon's rooms. The news spread round the farm like wildfire. The banknotes（钞票） were forgeries（伪造）! Frederick had got the timber for nothing! Napoleon called the animals together and in a terrible voice gave the death sentence on Frederick. When caught, Frederick should be boiled alive. He warned them that after this treacherous（背叛） act the worst was to come. Frederick and his men might attack at any moment. Sentinels were placed at all the ways to the farm. Also, four pigeons were sent to Foxwood with a friendly message, which it was hoped might make good relations with Pilkington again. The very next morning the attack came.

[P19] The animals were eating breakfast when the look-outs ran in with news that Frederick and his men had come through the five-barred（阻挡） gate. The animals went out bravely to meet them, but this time they did not win easily. There were fifteen men, with six guns, and they fired as soon as they were fifty yards away. The animals could not face the terrible explosions（爆炸） and the stinging（刺痛） pellets（颗粒）, and even with Napoleon and Boxer trying to rally（集会） them, they were soon driven back. Some were already wounded.

[P20] They hid in the farm buildings and looked out carefully through small holes. The big field, with the windmill, now belonged to the enemy. Even Napoleon did not know what to do. He walked up and down without a word, his tail stiff and moving. They looked sadly toward Foxwood. If Pilkington and his men helped them, they might still win. But just then the four pigeons they had sent out the day before came back. One carried a small piece of paper from Pilkington. On it he had written: "Serves you right." Meanwhile Frederick and his men had stopped near the windmill.

[P21] The animals watched them, and a murmur（低语） of dismay（沮丧） went round. Two men had brought out a crowbar（铁撬） and a sledge（大锤） hammer（锤子）. They were going to knock the windmill down. "Impossible!""Impossible!" cried Napoleon. "We have built the walls far too thick for that. They could not knock it down in a week. Courage, comrades!" But Benjamin was watching the men closely. The two men were drilling（钻孔） a hole near the base of the windmill. Slowly, Benjamin nodded his long muzzle（口鼻部）. "I thought so," he said. "Do you not see what they are doing?"

[P22] In another moment they will put blasting（爆破） powder（火药） into that hole." drill（钻头） muzzle blasting powder The animals were very afraid and waited. They could not leave the shelter now. After a few minutes, the men ran in all directions. Then came a loud roar. The pigeons flew up, and all the animals, except Napoleon, threw themselves flat and hid their faces. When they stood up, a huge cloud of black smoke hung where the windmill had been. Slowly the breeze blew it away. The windmill was gone! Seeing this, the animals felt brave again.

[P23] The fear and despair（绝望） they felt a moment ago were drowned in their anger at this evil act. A mighty（强大） cry for revenge（复仇） went up. Without waiting for more orders, they charged（冲锋） out together and went straight for the enemy. This time they did not care about the cruel pellets that swept over them like hail（冰雹）. It was a wild, bitter battle. The men fired again and again, and, when the animals got close, hit out with their sticks and heavy boots. A cow, three sheep, and two geese were killed, and almost everyone was wounded. Even Napoleon, who was directing the fight from the back, had the tip（尖端） of his tail cut by a pellet（弹丸）.

[P24] But the men were hurt too. Boxer's hoofs（蹄） broke the heads of three men. A cow's horn gored（刺伤） one man in the belly. Jessie and Bluebell nearly tore off another man's trousers. Napoleon had told his nine bodyguard（保镖） dogs to go a long way round behind the hedge（树篱）. Now they suddenly came at the men's side, barking fiercely, and the men were very afraid. They saw they might be surrounded（包围）. Frederick shouted to his men to run away while they could, and the next moment the cowardly（胆小） enemy was running for their lives. The animals chased（追赶） them to the bottom of the field, and kicked them a few last times as they pushed through the thorn（荆棘） hedge. They had won, but they were tired and bleeding.

[P25] Slowly they limped（跛行） back to the farm. Seeing their dead friends on the grass made some cry. For a while they stood in sad silence where the windmill had stood. It was gone — almost the last mark of their labour（劳作）! Even the base was partly destroyed. This time they could not rebuild it with the fallen stones. The stones had vanished（消失） too. The explosion（爆炸） had thrown them hundreds of yards away. It was as if the windmill had never been. Near the farm, Squealer, who had been away during the fighting for no clear reason, came jumping towards them, wagging（摇摆） his tail and smiling with joy.

[P26] And the animals heard a deep boom（轰鸣） of a gun from the farm buildings. "What is that gun firing for?" said Boxer. "To celebrate our victory!" cried Squealer. "What victory?" said Boxer. His knees were bleeding, and many small shots had gone into his back leg. "What victory, comrade? Have we not driven the enemy off our soil—the sacred（神圣） soil of Animal Farm?" "But they have destroyed the windmill. And we worked on it for two years!" "What matter? We will build another windmill. We will build six windmills（风车） if we feel like it.

[P27] "You do not understand, comrade, the great thing we have done. The enemy held this very ground we stand on. And now—thanks to the leadership of Comrade Napoleon—we have won every inch of it back!" "Then we have won back what we had before," said Boxer. "That is our victory," said Boxer.said Squealer. They limped into the yard. The pellets under Boxer's leg hurt badly. He saw ahead the heavy work of rebuilding the windmill, and he braced（撑住） himself for it. But for the first time he felt that he was eleven years old and his muscles（肌肉） were not what they had been. But when the animals saw the green flag flying, heard the gun fire seven times, and heard Napoleon's speech congratulating them, it seemed to them that they had won a great victory.

[P28] The animals killed in the battle had a solemn（庄严） funeral. Boxer and Clover pulled the wagon（货车） that served as a hearse（灵车）, and Napoleon walked at the head. Two whole days were given to celebrations（庆祝）, with songs, speeches, and more firing of the gun. Every animal got a gift of an apple, each bird two ounces（盎司） of corn, and each dog three biscuits. It was announced that the battle would be called the Battle of the Windmill, and that Napoleon had created a new decoration（装饰）, the Order of the Green Banner（横幅）, which he gave to himself.

[P29] In the general joy, the bad business of the banknotes was forgotten. A few days later, the pigs found a case of whisky（威士忌） in the cellars（地窖） of the farmhouse. It was missed when the house was first taken. That night, loud singing came from the farmhouse. To everyone's surprise, the tune of 'Beasts（野兽） of England' was mixed in. At about half past nine, Napoleon, wearing an old bowler hat of Mr. Jones's, was clearly seen to come out of the back door, run quickly round the yard, and go inside again.

[P30] But in the morning a deep silence hung over the farmhouse. No pig seemed to be moving. It was nearly nine o'clock when Squealer appeared, walking slowly and sadly, his eyes dull（沉闷）, his tail hanging limply（无力）. He called the animals together and told them he had terrible news. Comrade Napoleon was dying（垂死）! A cry of sorrow（悲伤） went up. Straw was put down outside the farmhouse doors, and the animals walked on tiptoe（踮脚）. With tears in their eyes they asked one another what they should do if their Leader were taken away.

[P31] A rumour（谣言） went round that Snowball had put poison（毒药） in Napoleon's food. At eleven o'clock Squealer came out to make another announcement（宣布）. Napoleon had made a decree（法令）: drinking alcohol（酒精） was to be punished by death. By the evening, Napoleon seemed a little better, and the next morning Squealer told them he was getting better. By the evening Napoleon was back at work, and the next day it was learned that he had told Whymper to buy in Willingdon some booklets（小册子） on brewing（酿造） and distilling（蒸馏）.

[P32] A week later, Napoleon ordered that the small field beyond the orchard（果园）, which was once planned as a resting place for old animals, must be ploughed up. People were told the grass was used up and needed new seed; but soon everyone knew Napoleon wanted to plant barley（大麦） there. Around this time, a strange thing happened that almost no one could understand. One night at about twelve o'clock, there was a loud crash（碰撞） in the yard, and the animals ran out of their stalls（畜栏）.

[P33] It was a moonlit（月光） night. At the foot of the barn's end wall, where the Seven Commandments（戒律） were written, a ladder lay broken in two. Squealer lay beside it, stunned（震惊）, and nearby lay a lantern, a paint-brush, and a pot of white paint turned over. The dogs at once circled Squealer and took him back to the farmhouse once he could walk. None of the animals understood what this meant, except old Benjamin, who nodded with a knowing air, and seemed to understand, but would say nothing. But a few days later Muriel, reading the Seven Commandments to herself, noticed another one which the animals had remembered wrong.

[P34] They remembered the Fifth Commandment as "No animal shall drink alcohol." But they forgot two words. It really said: "No animal shall drink alcohol TO EXCESS（过量）."
